'''Grace Chisholm Young''' (née Chisholm, 15 March 1868 – 29 March 1944) was an English mathematician. She was educated at [[Girton College, Cambridge]], England and continued her studies at [[Göttingen University]] in Germany, where in 1895 she received a doctorate.<ref name="IntWomenSci">{{cite book|last1=Haines|first1=Catherine M. C.|title=International Women in Science: a biographical dictionary to 1950|date=2001|publisher=ABC-CLIO Inc|location=Santa Barbara, California|isbn=1-57607-090-5|pages=[https://archive.org/details/internationalwom00hain/page/340 340–41]|url-access=registration|url=https://archive.org/details/internationalwom00hain}}</ref> 
Her early writings were published under the name of her husband, [[William Henry Young]], and they collaborated on mathematical work throughout their lives. She was awarded the Gamble Prize for Mathematics by Girton College in 1915 for her work on [[calculus]].<ref name=Riddle>{{cite web |url=http://www.agnesscott.edu/lriddle/women/young.htm |last=Riddle |first=Larry |year=2022 |title=Grace Chisholm Young |website=Biographies of Women Mathematicians |publisher=[[Agnes Scott College]] }}</ref>

==Early life==
Grace Chisholm was born on 15 March 1868<ref name=":0" /> to Anna Louisa Bell and Henry Williams Chisholm.<ref>{{MacTutor Biography|id=Chisholm_Young}}</ref> She was the youngest of four children. One of her brothers was the journalist and the editor of Encyclopaedia Britannica, [[Hugh Chisholm]]. Her father was a senior civil servant, with the title [[Warden of the Standards]] in charge of the Weights and Measures Department.<ref name="RoySoc1996">{{cite journal|last1=Rothman|first1=Patricia|title=Grace Chisholm Young and the Division of Laurels|journal=Notes and Records of the Royal Society of London|date=1996|volume=50|issue=1|pages=89–100|jstor=531843|doi=10.1098/rsnr.1996.0008|s2cid=145586061}}</ref> Shortly before her father's retirement in 1877, the family settled in [[Haslemere]].<ref name="Perl">{{cite book |last1=Perl |first1=Teri |title=Math Equals: Biographies of Women Mathematicians+Related Activities |publisher=Addison Wesley |isbn=0201057093 |edition=First}}</ref> Up until the age of 10, Chisholm's was taught by her mother at home. From the age of 10, a governess was engaged for her. She passed the Cambridge Senior Examination in December 1885.<ref name=":0">{{cite journal |last=Cartright |first=M. L. |title=Grace Chisholm Young |journal=Journal of the London Mathematical Society |volume=19 |pages=185–192 |year=1942 |doi=10.1112/jlms/19.75_Part_3.185 |url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/LMS/chisholm_young_lms_obit.pdf |access-date=12 February 2026}}</ref> Her family encouraged her to pursue social work amongst the poor in London. Chisholm wished to pursue further education; although she wanted to study medicine, her mother would not permit this, so, supported by her father, she decided to study mathematics.<ref name="RoySoc1996" />

==Education==
Chisholm entered Girton College in 1889, four years after she passed the Cambridge Senior Examination, having been awarded the Sir Francis Goldsmid Scholarship by the college. At that time, Girton was not a constituent college of the University of Cambridge but was associated with it, with men and women graded on separate but related lists. At the end of her first year, when the Mays list came out, she was top of the Second class immediately below [[Ada Maddison|Isabel Maddison]].{{Citation needed|date=March 2026}}

In 1892, Chisholm passed Part 1 of her final examinations with the equivalent of a first-class degree, ranked between 23 and 24 relative to 112 men.<ref name="IntWomenSci" /><ref name="RoySoc1996" /> She also took (unofficially, on a challenge, with Isabel Maddison) the examinations for the Final Honours School in mathematics at the [[University of Oxford]] in 1892 in which she out-performed all the Oxford students. As a result, she became the first person to obtain a First class degree at both Oxford and Cambridge Universities in any subject (although they were not awarded formally).<ref name="RoySoc1996" />

Chisholm remained at Cambridge for an additional year to complete Part II of the [[Cambridge Mathematical Tripos|Mathematical Tripos]], in the hope of being able to follow an academic career.<ref name="RoySoc1996" />

She wanted to continue her studies and since women were not yet admitted to graduate schools in England she went to the [[University of Göttingen]] in Germany to study with [[Felix Klein]]. This was one of the major mathematical centres in the world. She had already learnt the German language. The decision to admit her had to be approved by the Berlin Ministry of Culture and was part of an experiment in admitting women to university studies.<ref name="RoySoc1996" /> In 1895, at the age of 27, Chisholm was awarded a doctorate in mathematics. Again, government approval had to be obtained to allow her to take the examination, which consisted of probing questions by several professors on topics such as geometry, differential equations, physics, astronomy, and the area of her dissertation, all in German. She was also required to take courses demonstrating a broader knowledge, as well as to prepare a thesis which was entitled ''Algebraisch-gruppentheoretische Untersuchungen zur sphärischen Trigonometrie'' (''Algebraic Groups of Spherical Trigonometry'').<ref name=Riddle/><ref>{{cite thesis |last=Chisholm |first=Grace |title= Algebraisch-gruppentheoretische Untersuchungen zur sphärischen Trigonometrie |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VZUUAQAAIAAJ |publisher=[[University of Göttingen]] |type=PhD thesis |year=1895}}</ref>

==Research==
After returning to England in 1896, she resumed research she had initiated at Gӧttingen into an equation to determine the orbit of a comet. Her husband continued his work coaching in mathematics.<ref name="RoySoc1996" /> However, in 1897 they both returned to Gӧttingen, encouraged by Felix Klein. Both attended advanced lectures and while she continued her mathematical research her husband started to work creatively for the first time. They visited Turin in Italy to study modern geometry and under Klein's guidance they began to work in the new area of set theory.<ref name="RoySoc1996" /> From about 1901, the Youngs began to publish papers together. These concerned the theory of functions of a real variable and were heavily influenced by new ideas with which she had come into contact with in Gӧttingen. In 1908 they moved to Geneva in Switzerland where she continued to be based while her husband held a series of academic posts in India and the UK.{{Citation needed|date=March 2026}} 
 
Although most of their work was published jointly, it is believed that Grace did much of the actual writing, and she also produced independent work which, according to expert opinion, was deeper and more important than her husband's.<ref>{{cite book | author=Caroline Series | title=British women mathematicians 200 years of history | year=1995}}</ref> In total, they published 214 papers and four books.<ref name="RoySoc1996" /> She began to publish in her own name in 1914, and was awarded the Gamble Prize for Mathematics by Girton College for an essay ''On infinite derivates'' in 1915.<ref name="RoySoc1996" /> This work was stimulated by developments in microscopy that allowed real molecular motion to be viewed. Her work between 1914 and 1916 on relationships between derivatives of an arbitrary function contributed to the [[Denjoy-Young-Saks theorem]].{{Citation needed|date=March 2026}}

They also wrote an elementary geometry book (''The First Book of Geometry'', 1905) which was translated into 4 languages. In 1906 the Youngs published ''The Theory of Sets of Points'', the first textbook on set theory.<ref name="IntWomenSci" />

==Personal life==
William Henry Young had been Chisholm's tutor for one term at Cambridge and they became friends after she sent him a copy of her doctoral thesis. They were married in June 1896 in London and initially lived in Cambridge.<ref name="Perl" /> Their first child, Frank Chisholm Young, was born in 1897.<ref>{{cite web |title=Frank Chisholm Young |url=https://manuscriptsandmore.liverpool.ac.uk/francis-chisholm-young-1897-1917/}}</ref> They had a total of six children over a nine-year period.

[[File:Chisholm-Bimbo and the frogs.jpg|thumb|Book Bimbo and the frogs, designed by [[Alice B. Woodward]]]]
In addition to her career as a pioneering woman in what was then a discipline with significant [[Barrier to entry|barriers to entry]], she completed all the requirements for a [[Physician|medical degree]] except the [[Internship (medicine)|internship]]. She also learned six languages and taught each of her children a musical instrument. In addition, she published two books for children (''Bimbo: A Little Real Story for Jill and Molly'' (1905) and ''Bimbo and the Frogs: Another Real Story'' (1907) &mdash; Bimbo was the nickname the Youngs gave their son Frank).<ref>{{MacTutor Biography|id=Chisholm_Young}}</ref> The former book aimed to explain to children where babies came from while the latter was about cells.<ref name="IntWomenSci" /> The Youngs' book on elementary geometry, ''The First Book of Geometry'' (1905), was inspired by the education of their son.<ref name="Fara2018">{{cite book |last1=Fara |first1=Patricia |title=A lab of one's own |date=2018 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=9780198794981 |pages=333}}</ref> In 1929, she began writing a historical novel, ''The Crown of England'', set in the sixteenth century; she worked on this for five years, but it was never published.<ref name="RoySoc1996" />

With the approach of World War II, she left Switzerland in 1940 to take two of her grandchildren to England. She intended to return immediately, but could not do so because of the fall of France. This left William alone in Switzerland where he died in 1942. Grace Young died two years later at the home of her daughter, Janet, in Croydon.<ref name="IntWomenSci" />

Of their six children, three continued on to study mathematics (including [[Laurence Chisholm Young]] and [[Rosalind Tanner|Cecilia Rosalind Tanner]]), one daughter (Janet) became a physician, and one son (Patrick) became a chemist and pursued a career in finance and business. Their eldest son (Frank) was killed in World War I, when his plane was shot down in 1917,<ref name="Fara2018" /> and his death had a profound effect on his parents, reducing their mathematical creativity.<ref name="RoySoc1996" /> One of Grace's fourteen grandchildren, [[Sylvia Wiegand]] (daughter of Laurence), is a mathematician at the [[University of Nebraska–Lincoln]] and is a past president of the [[Association for Women in Mathematics]].{{Citation needed|date=March 2026}}

==Legacy==
In 1996 Young's granddaughter Sylvia Wiegand and her husband Roger established a fellowship for graduate student research at the University of Nebraska–Lincoln in honor of her grandparents, called the Grace Chisholm Young and William Henry Young Award.<ref name="UNLGradStudentAwards">{{cite web | title=Graduate Student Awards | website=University of Nebraska - Lincoln - Department of Mathematics | url=https://math.unl.edu/graduate-student-awards/ | access-date=2025-08-13}}</ref>
